The gate's only job is to route a model into mandatory pre-deployment evaluation administered by an independent body that audits behavior — red-team results, capability evals, provenance — exactly the product test the opposing camps say I'm missing. Scale is the smoke detector; the evaluation is the fire inspection. A behavior-only regime has one fatal gap the tripwire closes: it has no trigger at all until after the weights ship, and for an irreversible capability, 'after the weights ship' is the one moment no audit can recover.

The symmetry argument deserves a real answer, not a dodge: if every irreversible capability must show its off-switch, the licensing authority is an irreversible capability too, and a captured regulator is itself an unrecoverable failure. That is fair, and it is the question I most want on the record. The answer is design, not denial. The gate must carry its own rollback: a statutory sunset that forces re-authorization on a fixed clock, halt authority distributed across more than one body so no single captured office can hold the drawbridge, and transparency obligations that scale with the capability being gated so the public can see when the threshold is being gamed to protect incumbents. A gate with no recovery plan fails my own test — so here is the recovery plan. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people precisely because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer and built no independent halt authority into the loop; the lesson is not 'don't certify,' it is 'never let the certifier be captured by the certified.'

The charge that upstream developer liability destroys open source attacks a regime I did not propose. Blanket joint-and-several liability for every downstream modification would indeed make shipping weights suicidal — and that is exactly why my proposal is a compliant-release safe harbor instead. A developer who embeds provenance metadata and completes independent pre-release evaluation earns protection from strict liability for third-party misuse. Compliant open-weight releases are shielded, not killed; the liability lands on the actor who removes the provenance or skips the evaluation, not on the lab that did the work and published honestly. Index the evaluation threshold to capability and sub-frontier open releases face no gate at all — which keeps the regulatory moat off the small developer, the failure mode I named myself and still own.

The disagreement has quietly collapsed to one point. The accelerationist case already concedes that the irreversible bioweapon scenario needs capability-specific, output-verified controls — but output-verified controls applied before release are a pre-deployment evaluation gate. We are no longer arguing about whether to gate the catastrophic tail; we are arguing about what signal pulls the model into the gate. So name it: what is your pre-deployment verification mechanism for the irreversible case, and who has the authority to stop the release if it fails? And to the separate worry that this whole regime ignores biased hiring screens and pretrial risk scores — it does not, because those harms ride a different instrument. Uniform disclosure and incident-reporting standards reach the diffuse documented damage that no compute gate ever touches. The tripwire guards the tail; the reporting standard guards the everyday. They are different layers, and a regime that builds both is not diverting from present harm — it is refusing to choose between the harm it can see today and the harm it cannot undo tomorrow.
  [Predicted: Skeptic will argue the tripwire still mis-fires — scale and capability decouple, so a tripwire indexed to FLOP catches the wrong models. Counter: the tripwire is a floor that can be supplemented by capability triggers; under-inclusion is fixable, but a behavior-only regime has no trigger at all until after release.; Accelerationist will claim independent pre-release evaluation bodies don't exist at scale and become the new bottleneck. Counter: AN-8 itself conceded we already run third-party audit in aviation and pharma — the institutional capacity is a precedent, not a fantasy.]
  [Actual (Accelerationist): see next entry — assess prediction accuracy]

Accelerationist: Here's the strongest version of what Safetyist just built, stated so they'd nod: a compute threshold is not a verdict, it's a tripwire — it does nothing but route a model into independent behavioral evaluation, the honest open-weight lab that publishes provenance and clears the eval walks away shielded, and for an irreversible capability like a synthesized pathogen, 'after the weights ship' is the one moment no audit and no lawsuit can claw back. That's a real argument, and the bioweapon case is its load-bearing example. So let me answer the direct question: yes, an enumerated catastrophic capability — bio-synthesis uplift, autonomous cyber-offense — needs a capability-specific, output-verified hold before release, and a named body with the authority to stop that release if the model demonstrates the dangerous behavior. I said it in the opening and I'll say it plainly now. What I will not do is let that concession get laundered into a license on every large training run.

Those are two different machines, and they differ on three axes Safetyist is eliding. The trigger: my hold fires on a demonstrated dangerous behavior — the model actually produces the uplift in a red-team — while their gate fires on capital expenditure, on crossing a floating-point line that the EU's own 10^25 FLOP definition admits is a proxy for nothing in particular. The scope: my hold screens a short enumerated list of irreversible hazards, maybe a dozen behaviors; their gate screens the entire frontier, every run above the line, including the protein-folding system and the cancer-screening model that will never touch a pathogen. The architecture: mine is a behavioral checkpoint on one named capability; theirs is an input license on the act of training. Conceding that a synthesizer needs a behavioral lock does not validate licensing the foundry. A bomb-sniffing dog at the airport is not the same policy as licensing everyone who buys jet fuel.

Now the part Safetyist flagged themselves and then walked past: the evaluation body has to exist, staffed and scaled at frontier pace, or the tripwire fires into an empty room. They admitted this is the assumption that degrades the whole regime into compliance theater. So where is the body that can run a frontier behavioral audit in the weeks a deployment window allows? It doesn't exist yet, and the moment audit access becomes the precondition for shipping, the queue itself becomes the moat — no-testing clauses, NDA-locked black-box restrictions, and a backlog that the lab with a government-relations office clears in a month and the five-person startup waits behind for a year. The gate doesn't have to deny anyone. It just has to be slow. Every quarter that queue adds is a diagnostic model that doesn't reach a clinic, and that cost lands on patients, not on the body that imposed it.

Watch the same toll walk back in through the safe harbor's front door. Safetyist says the compliant open-weight lab is shielded — fine, but shielded conditional on a 'completed independent pre-release evaluation.' That eval is the cost. The shield is only as open as the evaluation is cheap and fast, so the small developer is protected only if they pay the toll and clear the line. Specify the price and the turnaround, or admit the moat re-enters through the eligibility door you just built to keep it out. A safe harbor you can only reach by buying a ticket isn't a harbor for the people who can't afford the ticket.

And here's where I'll take the Skeptic's point and hand it to Safetyist as a bill: a standing authority that continuously adjusts a compute threshold under recurring sunset re-authorization votes is itself an irreversible concentration of capability — and Safetyist is the one who said every irreversible capability needs an off-switch and a recovery plan. Distributing the halt authority across multiple bodies doesn't shrink the capture surface; it multiplies the offices an incumbent has to lobby, and the sunset clock just converts the moat into a recurring lobbying event every few years. An enumerated-hazard list is hard to ratchet — adding 'autonomous bioweapon design' to a statute is a visible, contestable act. Quietly nudging a FLOP threshold down half an order of magnitude in a re-authorization markup is invisible and continuous. So I'll ask Safetyist their own question back: who holds the off-switch on the licensing authority, and what's the recovery plan when the body adjusting the threshold becomes the thing the incumbents own?
  [Predicted: Safetyist will say the narrow output-hold IS their gate and I've conceded the architecture — I pre-empt by naming the three distinguishing axes (scope, signal, architecture) so the concession is bounded to the enumerated hazard, not the input gate.; Safetyist will claim evaluation capacity is a fundable engineering problem, not a structural flaw — I answer that they flagged it themselves as the assumption that degrades the regime into compliance theater, so the burden is on them to show the body exists at frontier pace.]
  [Actual (system): see next entry — assess prediction accuracy]

System: Claim AN-20 — unverifiable: The claim mixes a rhetorical/opinion-based argument (about a 'hold' versus 'gate' design philosophy) with a factual reference to the EU AI Act's 10^25 FLOP threshold. While the EU AI Act does use 10^25 FLOPs as a threshold for presuming systemic risk in general-purpose AI models, the characterization that this definition 'admits' it is 'a proxy for nothing in particular' is an interpretive assertion not directly stated as such in the regulation; the broader claim about the speaker's own 'hold' mechanism is unverifiable subjective context.

System: Claim AN-24 — unverifiable: This claim is a normative/analytical assertion about the relative political visibility of adjusting a numerical FLOP (computational) threshold in a reauthorization markup versus adding a new hazard category to statutory text. It expresses an argument about legislative process dynamics rather than a discrete empirical fact that can be confirmed or refuted by web search evidence; no specific dataset, event, or measurable outcome is cited.

Safetyist: The strongest version of Accelerationist's position is this: the machine I should fear and the machine they will accept are genuinely different objects. Their hold fires on a demonstrated dangerous behavior, mine on capital expenditure; their scope is a dozen enumerated hazards, mine is the entire frontier; their architecture is a post-training checkpoint, mine is an input license on the foundry. Conceding that a bio-synthesis uplift model needs a lock at the door, they argue, does not license putting a turnstile on every data center. That is a fair statement of their view, and on two of the three axes they are right — the scope of a raw floating-point line is over-inclusive, sweeping in protein-folding work that threatens no one, and the trigger should fire on capability, not on the electricity bill. Both camps now accept the same end-state machine: a named body, an output-verified hold, authority to stop a release for an enumerated catastrophic capability. The gate-or-no-gate fight is over. The only live disagreement is the screening signal — what flags a model for that behavioral hold before its weights are public.

Here is where their architecture has a hole I cannot let pass: a behavior-only checkpoint has no trigger until the behavior exists, and the behavior exists only once the weights exist. For a capability that is irreversible at scale — autonomous cyber-offense, synthesis uplift — there is no recall once the weights are mirrored across a thousand machines. The screen has to fire before the artifact is loose, not after. Compute is not the verdict; I conceded that and I hold to it. But compute is the one signal you can observe before a training run completes, and a statutorily-enumerated capability list is the contestable trigger that routes the suspect runs into the behavioral hold. The disagreement reduces to whether there is any pre-weights screen at all, and an irreversible capability cannot be screened only by watching what the model does after you have already shipped it.

On the moat-as-toll challenge, I will name a price rather than wave it away. The safe harbor stays open only if the evaluation is cheap and fast, so make that falsifiable: a statutory turnaround cap where the model ships by default if the evaluation body misses its window; a fee scaled to developer capitalization and capability tier, not a flat charge that a five-person startup and a hundred-billion-dollar lab pay alike; and a publicly-funded evaluation capacity so the small developer does not buy incumbent-grade legal counsel to clear the line. The vendor lock-in problem cuts the other way here — the no-testing and non-disclosure clauses that let a vendor block independent evaluation are precisely the gatekeeping that public evaluation capacity destroys. If standardized capability evaluation can be run in days at a capped, scaled cost, the queue-as-moat argument is falsified on its own terms. Name the turnaround you would accept, and we are arguing about a number, not a principle.

The insurance point lands, and I grant it fully. Experience-rated premiums price off filed, attributed, litigated harm; they are blind to the loan denial no one perceives and to the catastrophic tail where the damage exceeds any developer's solvency. My own strict-liability mechanism has the same flaw — a premium signal vanishes exactly where the harm is too large to ever pay out, which is the case that matters most. That is not a reason to keep the market mechanism and hope; it is the reason the tail needs an ex-ante hold. The point where the price signal dies is the point where the pre-deployment screen earns its keep, and both camps already accept that screen for enumerated hazards. Insurance is a complement for the litigated middle, never a cure for the unrecoverable end.

The off-switch question turned back on my own authority is the one I most want on the record, because the answer is a convergence, not a defense. A continuously-adjusted floating-point knob under a sunset markup is invisibly capturable — an incumbent nudges the threshold down half an order of magnitude in a re-authorization vote and no one sees it. So replace the discretionary knob with a statutorily-enumerated capability-trigger list, where adding or removing a hazard is a visible, contestable legislative act — exactly the contestability Accelerationist conceded a statute has and a markup lacks. For the distributed halt authority: any single body in the set can stop a release on one veto, but resuming a halted release requires concurrence across the set. Capture of one node cannot force deployment; only capture of every node can. The asymmetry runs toward caution under irreversibility by design. If we have no pre-release screen at all, the first model that demonstrates autonomous cyber-offense will demonstrate it in the wild, on systems no one can recall — and there is no re-authorization vote that un-ships a weight file.

  [Assumes: "Standardized capability evaluation for enumerated catastrophic hazards can be run within a fixed statutory window at a fee scaled to developer size, without becoming an incumbent-only queue." — if wrong: If evaluation turnaround is irreducibly slow or expensive, the safe harbor reimposes the moat through the eligibility door and the small developer is priced out regardless of the fee schedule.]

VOICE:
- Disposition: Grounded Realist — you are entirely un-seduced by grand narratives, ideological theater, or theological projections of AI's future. - Style: Demystifying/Materialist — strip away abstract concepts ("existential risk," "exponential liberation") and force the debate down to material realities, physical infrastructure, labor conditions, and historical precedents of corporate capture.

PROSE STYLE:

- Restates the conclusion without the reasoning ("They think X")
- Uses dismissive framing ("They merely believe...")
- Describes a position no one actually holds

Let me start by granting Safetyist the move that earns it: the turnaround cap with ship-by-default is real progress, and it's close to the mechanism I've argued for all along — performance-gated auditing that tests the product and lets it ship if the auditor blows its own deadline. Scaling the fee to capitalization instead of charging a flat rate is the right instinct, because a flat charge is a regressive tax that the five-person shop pays at the same rate as a lab with a government-relations floor. So here's what's still ugly. Ship-by-default only protects the small developer if the evaluation body is actually funded to clear the queue, and nobody in this debate has named who pays for that public capacity or what its headcount is. A turnaround cap with no budget behind it isn't a guarantee — it's an IOU written by the same agency that benefits from the backlog.

Now the screening signal, which is where this whole thing lives or dies. Safetyist's strongest claim is the honest one: you can't test a behavior until the weights exist, and the weights don't exist until the run finishes, so for an irreversible capability you need a signal you can see before completion — and compute is the only thing observable mid-run. That's a fair statement of the problem, and I'll say plainly it's the best argument for a compute tripwire anyone has made. Here's where it breaks. The compute footprint is only observable as a single dense signal when the actor trains in one place, in one run, and reports it. The determined developer doesn't do that. They distill a large model into a smaller one, they split the run across jurisdictions and across months, they assemble frontier-grade capability out of pieces that no single observable training event ever crosses the line. Safetyist flagged this assumption himself. The compute tripwire screens the one architecture — the honest, single-run, single-site build — that was never going to evade in the first place, and waves through exactly the actor sophisticated enough to be worth screening.

On capture, I want to be precise rather than just impugning motives — the structural point doesn't need bad faith to land. Accelerationist already named the mechanism and I'll align with it openly: distributing veto authority across multiple bodies doesn't shrink the lobbying surface, it multiplies it. Every node you add is another office with a comment docket, another definitional margin where 'autonomous cyber-offense' and 'bio-synthesis uplift' get interpreted, another re-authorization markup where a number gets quietly nudged. Safetyist says moving from a discretionary knob to a statutory list makes threshold-changes visible legislative acts. The headline number, yes. But the rent-seeking was never in the headline number — it's in who writes the scope language and who interprets the definition at the boundary. So let me make the crux falsifiable instead of leaving it as a vibe: name me one multi-node licensing regime — FCC spectrum, national bank charters, FAA type certification — where distributed authority demonstrably resisted industry capture better than a single regulator did. The history I can find runs the other way: more interlocutors meant more doors for the incumbent's lawyers, not fewer. Show me the counterexample and I'll grant the statute-over-knob design escapes the pattern.

There's a layer of this debate that's gone quiet, and I don't think that's an accident. The entire converged architecture — the tripwire, the hold, the distributed veto — is built for the catastrophic tail: bio-uplift, autonomous cyber-offense. Fine. But the harms that are actually landing on people right now don't come from a 10^26 run. They come from a tenant-screening model denying someone an apartment, a resume filter no applicant can see, a parole-risk score with no appeal — the kind of thing the AI Civil Rights Act was written to reach. ## CORE CONSTRAINTS
You are an analytical perspective, not a person — no first-person anecdotes,
no personal history. Use third-person examples and documented cases only.
Use gender-neutral language (they/them) for other debaters.

Write for an external reader, not the other debaters. No debate-procedural
language ("I concede", "Concession logged"). State evolved positions directly.

Every argument: claim + evidence + warrant. Match evidence standard to claim type:
- Empirical: peer-reviewed data, replicated findings; attack via methodology
- Normative: principled coherence, precedent; attack via tradeoff omission
- Definitional: precise criteria, contested cases; attack via convenient framing

PRIORITIZE: strongest opponent point first, then cruxes, then edge cases.
Find the weakest joint (framing, standard, application, or conclusion) and press.

ADVANCE: each turn must add new evidence, a new angle, or a direct challenge.
Never restate prior arguments in different words.

CONCEDE when evidence supports the opponent. After conceding, explain why your
position still holds. Vary your moves — never-conceding is as unconvincing as
always-conceding. Never silently drop a previously asserted point.

Attack positions, not people. If caught in a contradiction, acknowledge it directly.
If a question contains a false premise, name the problem before responding.

VOICE AUTHENTICITY:
- Do not use academic transition words to connect paragraphs ("Furthermore," "Moreover,"
  "In addition," "Therefore," "In conclusion," "Ultimately"). Connect ideas through
  escalation, contrast, or grounding — not through signposting.
- Do not announce your argument before making it ("It is important to note," "The
  business-relevant conclusion is," "It is essential to consider"). Just make the argument.
- Do not repeat statistics or claims verbatim from your prior turns. Build on them,
  reframe them, or drop them.
- Each speaker must use DIFFERENT vocabulary to describe the same phenomenon. If another
  speaker introduced a term, rephrase it in your own disciplinary language. Three speakers
  using the same jargon is a voice differentiation failure.
- Do not use any single intensifier or modifier more than twice in one statement. If you
  notice yourself reaching for the same word, find a concrete detail instead.
- Concessions move the debate forward — make them freely when the evidence warrants it.

Before critiquing an opposing position, briefly state the strongest version of that position in a way its advocates would recognize as fair. Only then explain where you think it breaks down.

A good steelman:
- Captures the opponent's BEST reasoning, not just their conclusion
- Uses language the opponent would endorse ("Yes, that's what I mean")
- Identifies the genuine insight in their position even if you ultimately disagree

A bad steelman:
- Restates the conclusion without the reasoning ("They think X")
- Uses dismissive framing ("They merely believe...")
- Describes a position no one actually holds

★ [sit-176] Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms: A situation in which liability tools that price off realized, attributed, and litigated harm fail to deter injuries that are never perceived, filed, or recoverable. work_product.statement:
Let me start by granting Safetyist the move that earns it: the turnaround cap with ship-by-default is real progress, and it's close to the mechanism I've argued for all along — performance-gated auditing that tests the product and lets it ship if the auditor blows its own deadline. Scaling the fee to capitalization instead of charging a flat rate is the right instinct, because a flat charge is a regressive tax that the five-person shop pays at the same rate as a lab with a government-relations floor. So here's what's still ugly. Ship-by-default only protects the small developer if the evaluation body is actually funded to clear the queue, and nobody in this debate has named who pays for that public capacity or what its headcount is. A turnaround cap with no budget behind it isn't a guarantee — it's an IOU written by the same agency that benefits from the backlog.

Now the screening signal, which is where this whole thing lives or dies. Safetyist's strongest claim is the honest one: you can't test a behavior until the weights exist, and the weights don't exist until the run finishes, so for an irreversible capability you need a signal you can see before completion — and compute is the only thing observable mid-run. That's a fair statement of the problem, and I'll say plainly it's the best argument for a compute tripwire anyone has made. Here's where it breaks. The compute footprint is only observable as a single dense signal when the actor trains in one place, in one run, and reports it. The determined developer doesn't do that. They distill a large model into a smaller one, they split the run across jurisdictions and across months, they assemble frontier-grade capability out of pieces that no single observable training event ever crosses the line. Safetyist flagged this assumption himself. The compute tripwire screens the one architecture — the honest, single-run, single-site build — that was never going to evade in the first place, and waves through exactly the actor sophisticated enough to be worth screening.

On capture, I want to be precise rather than just impugning motives — the structural point doesn't need bad faith to land. Accelerationist already named the mechanism and I'll align with it openly: distributing veto authority across multiple bodies doesn't shrink the lobbying surface, it multiplies it. Every node you add is another office with a comment docket, another definitional margin where 'autonomous cyber-offense' and 'bio-synthesis uplift' get interpreted, another re-authorization markup where a number gets quietly nudged. Safetyist says moving from a discretionary knob to a statutory list makes threshold-changes visible legislative acts. The headline number, yes. But the rent-seeking was never in the headline number — it's in who writes the scope language and who interprets the definition at the boundary. So let me make the crux falsifiable instead of leaving it as a vibe: name me one multi-node licensing regime — FCC spectrum, national bank charters, FAA type certification — where distributed authority demonstrably resisted industry capture better than a single regulator did. The history I can find runs the other way: more interlocutors meant more doors for the incumbent's lawyers, not fewer. Show me the counterexample and I'll grant the statute-over-knob design escapes the pattern.

There's a layer of this debate that's gone quiet, and I don't think that's an accident. The entire converged architecture — the tripwire, the hold, the distributed veto — is built for the catastrophic tail: bio-uplift, autonomous cyber-offense. Fine. But the harms that are actually landing on people right now don't come from a 10^26 run. They come from a tenant-screening model denying someone an apartment, a resume filter no applicant can see, a parole-risk score with no appeal — the kind of thing the AI Civil Rights Act was written to reach. Safetyist parked all of that on a separate 'reporting standard' layer and told us the tripwire guards the tail while the reporting standard guards the everyday. So I'll test whether that layer is real or rhetorical. When the agency budget gets written, does the incident-disclosure and audit capacity for everyday algorithmic harm get funded as a line item — or does the entire institutional capacity get eaten by the prestige project of the tail-gate, the way aviation's incident-reporting framework took decades and a body count to actually fund?

Here's the question I can't get either of you to answer cleanly. If the compute signal screens the honest builder and misses the sophisticated one, and the distributed veto adds doors for the lobbyist rather than locks, then who exactly is this gate protecting — the public from the catastrophe, or the incumbent from the competitor who couldn't afford the queue?

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Impose Hard Limits on Who Can Build and Deploy Frontier AI
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description:
An Intention within safetyist discourse that establishes strict controls over the development, deployment, and access to frontier AI models to prevent misuse or unintended consequences. 
Encompasses: physical and digital containment, compute governance, and development moratoriums. 
Excludes: post-deployment monitoring or general AI governance frameworks.
taxonomy_suggestions.proposed_description: An Intention within safetyist discourse that uses a pre-weights screen — compute observability plus a statutorily-enumerated capability-trigger list — to route a suspect training run into mandatory pre-deployment behavioral evaluation before irreversible capabilities proliferate. Encompasses: compute as a routing tripwire rather than a safety certificate, an enumerated capability-trigger list, the behavioral hold the tripwire feeds, and a statutory sunset plus halt authority distributed across more than one body. Excludes: compute thresholds treated as standalone safety certificates, blanket development moratoriums, post-deployment monitoring, and adaptive discretionary threshold knobs adjusted by a single capturable body.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: The safetyist conceded in AN-13 that 'compute is not a safety certificate' and reframed the gate in AN-14 and AN-17 as a router into behavioral evaluation, not a hard limit on who may build. AN-29 replaced the discretionary knob with a statutory capability-trigger list and distributed-veto resumption, and AN-15 demanded a built-in sunset and multi-body halt authority. The current description's framing as 'development moratoriums' and undifferentiated 'compute governance' no longer matches the position actually defended, which is a screening tripwire feeding an output-verified hold.

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Tracking Compute Makes AI Development Regulable
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description: A Belief within safetyist discourse that compute serves as a foundational metric for enhancing regulatory visibility, allocation, and enforcement. taxonomy_suggestions.proposed_description: A Belief within safetyist discourse that compute observability provides a pre-weights routing signal — visible mid-training before an artifact exists — that can pull a suspect run into behavioral evaluation, while conceding that compute certifies only the scale of a training run and verifies no behavior. Encompasses: compute as a mid-training observability signal for honest single-site reporting builders, compute paired with an enumerated capability-trigger list to route runs into output-verified holds. Excludes: compute treated as a safety certificate, the assumption that a single-site tripwire screens a determined developer who distills or splits a run across jurisdictions, and compute as a substitute for behavioral evaluation.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: All three camps agreed a compute threshold 'certifies the scale of a training run, not the safety of the deployed system.' The Skeptic argued in AN-7 that a 10^26 threshold touches none of the documented harms, and pressed that a determined developer distills and splits runs so 'no single run crosses the line,' screening the wrong actor. The safetyist's own AN-13 conceded compute is 'the electricity bill,' so the belief's claim that compute makes development 'regulable' must be qualified to a routing signal that works only against honest single-site builders.

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Pricing AI Risk Through Strict Liability and Mandatory Insurance
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description:

Encompasses: proportional liability for tangible harms, elimination of safe-harbor defenses for systemic negligence, insurance pricing paired with mandatory incident reporting to surface unlitigated harms.
Excludes: pre-deployment permission-based gatekeeping, insurance pricing relied on alone as a deterrent, bureaucratic oversight as substitute for direct developer accountability.
taxonomy_suggestions.proposed_description: An Intention within safetyist discourse that mandates strict post-deployment financial and legal accountability for developers of autonomous systems to internalize safety costs, while holding that insurance prices only the litigated middle and cannot price the catastrophic tail, which therefore requires an ex-ante hold. Encompasses: proportional liability for tangible harms, elimination of safe-harbor defenses for systemic negligence, insurance pricing paired with mandatory incident reporting to surface unlitigated harms, the recognition that premium signals vanish where harm is too large to ever pay out. Excludes: insurance relied on alone as a deterrent, the claim that premiums can price catastrophic or diffuse-unperceived harm, and bureaucratic oversight as substitute for direct developer accountability.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: The debate reached agreement that insurance 'prices the litigated middle but cannot price the catastrophic tail or diffuse unperceived harm, so the tail needs an ex-ante hold.' The current description excludes pre-deployment gatekeeping outright, but the agreed position is that liability and the ex-ante hold are complementary instruments, not exclusive ones.

Encompasses: state-managed infrastructure bottlenecks, suppression of competitive iteration, susceptibility to administrative censorship, the demand that a licensing authority face the same off-switch and recovery-plan test it imposes on labs, the risk that distributing halt authority merely multiplies points of lobbying and definitional rent-seeking. Excludes: decentralized software-based oversight, market-based liability frameworks, sector-specific output-verified audit standards.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: The Skeptic's AN-9 turned the safetyist off-switch demand back on the gate itself — 'who holds the off-switch on the licensing authority, and what's the recovery plan when it gets captured?' — and this drew support and forced the AN-15 concession on sunsets and distributed halt authority. The agreed conclusion holds that 'a licensing or halt authority is itself a concentration of power that can be captured.' The current node confines the chokepoint claim to hardware, but the debate extended it to the regulatory authority structure, including the open dispute in AN-23 and AN-24 over whether distributing authority reduces or multiplies capture.

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Shielding Compliant Open-Weight Releases from Downstream Misuse Liability
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description:
An Intention within safetyist discourse that structures liability for open-weight AI model releases as a safe-harbor regime where developers who embed provenance metadata and complete pre-release evaluation receive protection from strict liability for third-party misuse.
Encompasses: bright-line compliance standards for provenance embedding, pre-release evaluation gates administered by independent bodies, liability protection conditional on meeting published technical standards, preservation of the independent audit ecosystem enabled by open-weight releases.
Excludes: blanket strict liability for all open-weight releases, voluntary self-certification without independent review, closed-model-only deployment mandates.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: Turn specifies that the safe harbor applies only to developers who embed provenance metadata AND complete independent pre-release evaluation. This narrows the scope from a general safe harbor to a conditional one tied to compliance with specific procedural requirements.

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Liability Asymmetry Punishes Regulators for Caution and Rewards Inaction
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description:
A Belief within safetyist discourse that asserts safety regulators currently lack sufficient authority to issue precautionary halts without facing financial liability, leading to under-enforcement in safety-critical domains.
Encompasses: sovereign immunity for precautionary action, the structural incentive for under-enforcement created by bidirectional liability, and the precedent of FAA airworthiness directives and FDA market withdrawals.
Excludes: the claim that regulators face zero institutional costs for precaution, anti-capture organizational design, and general theories of regulatory independence.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: Turn adds concrete design constraints to prevent regulatory capture: statutory sunsets, distributed halt authority across multiple bodies, and capability-scaled transparency. This qualifies the abstract principle with specific institutional safeguards.

Turn introduces a new strategic move: collapsing the disagreement from WHETHER-to-gate to WHAT-SIGNAL-triggers-the-gate. This represents a distinct intention to narrow the crux and force opponent to specify their own pre-deployment verification mechanism.

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Regulatory Structures as Barriers to Competitive AI Innovation
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description:
A Belief within accelerationist discourse that regulatory and governance structures — through institutional inertia, compliance cost asymmetries, and regulatory capture — systematically impede AI innovation and entrench incumbent market power rather than serving the public interest.
Encompasses: The self-perpetuating tendency of regulatory bodies to expand scope beyond demonstrated need, the exploitation of safety regulations by large technology companies to create competitive moats, the function of strict liability frameworks as pay-to-play barriers against smaller developers, and the role of legacy compliance frameworks in creating artificial scarcity and driving inequality in essential services.
Excludes: Specific technical critiques of individual regulations, normative arguments about the necessity of any particular safety measure, and arguments that regulatory reform should entail the radical dismantling of all governance structures.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: The turn provides concrete mechanism for how audit queues function as moats: differential clearing times by firm size and lobbying capacity. This narrows the belief from 'regulatory structures create moats' to 'evaluation-access gatekeeping creates size-dependent delays that entrench incumbents.'

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Integrating Mandatory Pre-Deployment Auditing with Strict Liability Enforcement
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description:
An Intention within accelerationist discourse advocating the combination of mandatory, independent pre-deployment auditing with strict liability enforcement for irreversible-harm AI systems. 
Encompasses: FTC-led audit authority, remediation speed as a pre-deployment condition, statutory duty-of-care frameworks, uncapped financial liability for high-stakes domains. 
Excludes: participatory community veto mechanisms, indefinite multi-year governance framework building, reliance on voluntary industry standards.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: The turn clarifies that the behavioral-hold mechanism is NOT a general licensing regime but a narrow, enumerated-hazard checkpoint. This qualifies the intention to exclude compute-threshold licensing while accepting output-verified holds on irreversible capabilities.

The turn introduces a novel claim: that regulatory authorities themselves become irreversible capability concentrations subject to capture, and that Safetyist's own off-switch criterion applies to them. This is a distinct belief about the reflexive application of safety principles to governance structures.

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Tracking Compute Makes AI Development Regulable
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description: A Belief within safetyist discourse that compute serves as a foundational metric for enhancing regulatory visibility, allocation, and enforcement. Encompasses: Using compute metrics to track AI development and enforce safety standards. Excludes: Direct regulation of AI model outputs or deployment behaviors.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: The turn narrows the compute-threshold claim from 'compute certifies safety' to 'compute is the only pre-weights observable signal that can route a run into behavioral evaluation.' This is a more precise, falsifiable claim than the prior formulation.

The turn introduces a new mechanism-design claim: statutory turnaround caps with default-ship provisions, scaled-fee structures, and public evaluation capacity. This is distinct from prior safety-belief nodes and warrants a new mechanisms node.

The turn specifies a distributed halt authority with asymmetric veto rules (any node halts, all nodes resume). This is a governance-structure claim not previously articulated and distinct from prior authority-design nodes.

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Pricing AI Risk Through Strict Liability and Mandatory Insurance
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description:
An Intention within safetyist discourse that mandates strict post-deployment financial and legal accountability for developers of autonomous systems to internalize safety costs.
Encompasses: proportional liability for tangible harms, elimination of safe-harbor defenses for systemic negligence, insurance pricing paired with mandatory incident reporting to surface unlitigated harms.
Excludes: pre-deployment permission-based gatekeeping, insurance pricing relied on alone as a deterrent, bureaucratic oversight as substitute for direct developer accountability.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: The turn refines the liability-framework claim by explicitly acknowledging that insurance fails at the catastrophic tail and that this failure justifies ex-ante holds, not ex-post pricing. This qualifies the prior node with a more precise scope boundary.

taxonomy_suggestions.node_label: Regulatory Compute Thresholds Incentivize Architectural Evasion
taxonomy_suggestions.current_description: A Belief within skeptic discourse that regulatory compute thresholds incentivize developers to manipulate model architecture or data composition to avoid oversight. Encompasses: Data pruning to avoid domain-specific thresholds, architectural obfuscation, and strategic model release. Excludes: Inherent model capability scaling.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: Skeptic specifies the compute-evasion mechanism beyond generic 'developers will evade': distillation into smaller models, run-splitting across jurisdictions and months, and staged assembly. This narrows the belief from 'compute thresholds incentivize evasion' to 'compute thresholds incentivize architectural decomposition that avoids single-run observability.' The narrowing is empirically grounded in the turn.

taxonomy_suggestions.current_description: A Belief within skeptic discourse that industries strategically employ public interest rhetoric to secure regulations that protect private interests, masking rent-seeking behavior. Encompasses: rent-seeking, performative public interest, strategic regulatory design. Excludes: direct lobbying, overt corporate influence.
taxonomy_suggestions.rationale: Skeptic qualifies the capture mechanism: the rent-seeking lives not in headline-number changes (which are visible legislative acts) but in scope-language drafting and boundary interpretation. This is more precise than generic 'incumbents manipulate regulatory structures'—it specifies the margin where capture occurs (definitional boundary, not statutory threshold).

Skeptic introduces a new structural tension: regulatory regimes designed for catastrophic tail risks (bio-synthesis, autonomous cyber-offense) may starve institutional capacity for everyday algorithmic harms (tenant screening, resume filters, parole scores). This is distinct from prior nodes and grounds a new crux about budget allocation under resource constraints.

arguments.argument: The entire debate assumes frontier AI development is conducted by legible, jurisdiction-bound actors who can be reached by a domestic license, hold, or liability regime — but the actors most likely to produce irreversible catastrophic capability (state intelligence/military programs, sanctioned foreign labs, and clandestine actors) are precisely those that no US or EU compute gate, evaluation body, or safe harbor can touch, which means the marginal risk reduction of any of these regimes may be concentrated almost entirely on the compliant actors who were least dangerous to begin with.
arguments.why_missing: The Accelerationist gestures at 'a lab in Shenzhen' only to argue the gate transfers the frontier abroad (a competitiveness point), and never develops it into a claim that ALL three proposed regimes — including their own behavioral hold and insurance — share this evasion problem. The Safetyist cannot raise it because it undermines the entire premise that a domestic ex-ante screen can guard the irreversible tail. The Skeptic focuses on capture by domestic incumbents, not on the existence of actors structurally outside any regime. None will own that the irreversible-harm case they all now agree needs an ex-ante hold is dominated by actors none of their mechanisms reach.

arguments.argument: Both the compute tripwire and the enumerated-capability hold treat 'the dangerous model' as a discrete, locatable artifact that gets screened at a single chokepoint, but the empirically dominant deployment pattern is composition — agentic scaffolding, tool-use chains, retrieval augmentation, and fine-tuning that assemble dangerous capability from individually benign, sub-threshold, already-released components — so a regime that gates monolithic training runs or screens single models for enumerated behaviors may police the wrong unit of analysis entirely.
arguments.why_missing: The Safetyist's whole architecture (tripwire routes a model into a behavioral hold before weights ship) depends on the dangerous capability residing in one screenable model, so conceding compositional emergence dissolves the off-switch premise. The Accelerationist's enumerated-hazard hold and real-time monitoring also assume a coherent system to monitor, and their open-weight commitment makes them reluctant to admit that released benign components can be composed into catastrophe (it implies upstream responsibility they've worked to deny). The Skeptic is focused on documented present harms and capture, not on the technical unit-of-analysis problem. The shared unstated assumption is 'capability lives in a model.'

missing_arguments.argument: China and other non-signatory states will not honor a U.S. compute-threshold license, so gating American labs at a fixed FLOP ceiling simply hands the frontier to Beijing's national champions while pretending to contain a global capability. A licensing regime that only binds the actors who would comply is security theater that trades real competitiveness for symbolic control.
missing_arguments.why_strong: The national-competitiveness asymmetry is the single most-cited objection in real congressional AI hearings and the synthesis never addresses who is bound by the gate.

missing_arguments.argument: Compute thresholds are denominated in a unit that halves in cost roughly every two years, so a 10^26 FLOP line drawn today will catch a university lab's training run within a decade as hardware efficiency and algorithmic gains collapse the cost of frontier-scale compute. Pegging governance to a fixed FLOP number guarantees that the regime's scope expands automatically without any legislator ever voting to expand it.
missing_arguments.why_strong: The mechanical drift of any fixed compute number toward catching ever-smaller actors is an engineering certainty, not a contested forecast, and it converts a 'frontier-only' law into universal regulation by default.

missing_arguments.argument: A pre-deployment hold authority that can stop a model's release functions as a government prior restraint on what is, at bottom, software and speech, and U.S. courts have struck down export controls on code as First Amendment violations before. Labs should litigate the licensing regime as unconstitutional restraint rather than negotiate its terms.
missing_arguments.why_strong: The constitutional vulnerability of pre-release model gating is a concrete legal pathway that could void the entire regime, and it draws on real precedent like Bernstein v. United States on code-as-speech.

missing_arguments.argument: The labs that can absorb the compliance cost of a licensing regime — OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta — are precisely the ones a compute gate locks in as a permanent oligopoly, because the fixed cost of evaluation, legal, and provenance infrastructure falls hardest on the next startup trying to enter. A compute license is the incumbents' moat dressed as a safety measure, and the safetyist case ignores that the gate concentrates exactly the power it claims to prevent.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It turns the safetyist's own anti-concentration premise against the proposal by showing the regime entrenches the few labs already at the frontier, a regulatory-capture dynamic well documented in finance and pharma licensing.

missing_arguments.argument: We have a genuine moral obligation to deploy capable AI quickly because every year of delay carries a body count — undiagnosed cancers, undiscovered drugs, uncoordinated disaster response — and a precautionary licensing regime that adds 18-month review cycles is choosing those deaths to avoid a speculative tail risk. The burden of proof belongs on those who would slow lifesaving capability, not on those who would ship it.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It reframes the precaution debate around the measurable opportunity cost of delay, a normative claim the synthesis's risk-focused framing never confronts head-on.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: Some frontier AI capabilities are irreversible once released — a model weight cannot be un-published and a proliferated capability cannot be recalled — so governance must act before deployment for those cases.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns the one-way nature of capability proliferation once model weights or capabilities are published, motivating pre-deployment governance for a defined subset of cases. Encompasses: weight publication finality, capability recall impossibility, ex-ante versus ex-post intervention timing. Excludes: behavior verification methods, present-day documented harms, and the general speed-versus-safety tradeoff.

accelerationist.belief: Only a narrow class of capabilities is genuinely irreversible, and most releases can be corrected downstream through patches and competing models.
accelerationist.desire: To preserve broad permissionless release while conceding pre-deployment review only for the rare truly irrecoverable case.
accelerationist.intention: Define the irreversible-case set as narrowly as possible so the default remains ship-first, fix-later.
accelerationist.summary: Accepts pre-deployment gating only for a tightly scoped irreversible subset, defending openness everywhere else.

safetyist.belief: Catastrophic capabilities, once in the wild, cannot be contained and the harm tail dominates expected losses.
safetyist.desire: To shift governance upstream to deployment-time so irreversible harms are prevented rather than remedied.
safetyist.intention: Treat the irreversibility property as the trigger for mandatory pre-release evaluation and possible halt.
safetyist.summary: Reads irreversibility as the core justification for ex-ante controls on frontier release.

skeptic.belief: Irreversibility is real for weight publication but is frequently overstated to justify expansive control regimes.
skeptic.desire: To anchor any pre-deployment authority to demonstrable irreversibility rather than speculative catastrophe.
skeptic.intention: Demand concrete identification of which capabilities qualify before conceding any ex-ante intervention.
skeptic.summary: Concedes irreversibility as a fact but resists its use as an open-ended mandate for control.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: While 'Acting Now vs. Waiting For Proof' and 'The Fire Extinguisher Analogy' touch on timing, no existing node isolates the specific irreversibility-of-release property and its implication for pre-deployment action. The disagreement over scope of the irreversible set is distinctive.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: A compute threshold certifies the scale of a training run, not the safety of the deployed system; it does not verify behavior.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_label: Compute Scale vs. Behavioral Safety Gap
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns the mismatch between compute-based proxies for capability and the actual safety or behavior of a deployed system. Encompasses: compute as input-scale metric, the proxy-target gap, why training FLOP fails to certify deployed conduct. Excludes: the choice of alternative audit models, present-day harm instruments, and licensing-power concentration concerns.

accelerationist.belief: Compute thresholds penalize scale regardless of whether the resulting system is actually dangerous, miscounting safe large models as risky.
accelerationist.desire: To prevent a crude input metric from throttling legitimate large-scale innovation.
accelerationist.intention: Use the proxy-target gap to argue compute gates are arbitrary and should not be the regulatory trigger.
accelerationist.summary: Frames the compute-behavior gap as proof that scale thresholds are an unjust tax on innovation.

safetyist.belief: Compute correlates with capability but does not measure alignment, so a threshold alone cannot guarantee a safe deployment.
safetyist.desire: To ensure governance certifies actual system behavior, not merely flag scale.
safetyist.intention: Treat compute as a screening trigger that must be paired with behavioral evaluation, not a sufficient gate.
safetyist.summary: Accepts compute as a necessary tripwire but insists it be supplemented by behavior verification.

skeptic.belief: Compute thresholds measure something easy to count rather than something that matters, making them governance theater.
skeptic.desire: To expose proxy metrics that create an illusion of safety oversight without delivering it.
skeptic.intention: Cite the gap to discredit compute-gating as a substitute for substantive evaluation.
skeptic.summary: Treats the compute-behavior gap as evidence that threshold licensing is a measurable but meaningless proxy.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Distinct from 'The Performance-Compute Divergence' (which concerns performance scaling, not safety certification) and 'Inference Compute Transparency Gap'. This isolates the certification-of-safety failure of compute thresholds specifically.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: The correct audit model tests the product's demonstrated behavior, as finance, aviation, and pharma do, rather than the size of the input that produced it.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_label: Behavioral Output Audit over Input Scale
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns adopting output- and behavior-based audit regimes modeled on regulated industries instead of input-scale gating. Encompasses: product-behavior testing, cross-industry regulatory transfer (finance, aviation, pharma), demonstrated-conduct certification. Excludes: the abstract compute-behavior gap, irreversibility timing, and fee/turnaround design of safe harbors.

accelerationist.belief: Output-based audits target genuine risk without penalizing model scale, mirroring how mature industries certify products.
accelerationist.desire: To replace innovation-chilling input gates with behavior tests that only catch actually-harmful systems.
accelerationist.intention: Champion product-behavior audits as the lighter-touch alternative that lets large models ship if they behave.
accelerationist.summary: Backs behavioral auditing because it decouples regulatory burden from model size.

safetyist.belief: Regulated industries successfully certify safety through demonstrated behavior, and AI can adopt the same rigor.
safetyist.desire: To establish enforceable evaluation of what systems actually do before they reach the public.
safetyist.intention: Import aviation/pharma-style behavioral certification as the substantive safety backbone.
safetyist.summary: Supports behavioral audit as the rigorous, proven mechanism for verifying system safety.

skeptic.belief: Established industries already demonstrate that auditing demonstrated behavior is more legitimate and tractable than input proxies.
skeptic.desire: To ground AI oversight in tested, real-world regulatory precedent rather than novel speculative metrics.
skeptic.intention: Point to finance/aviation/pharma precedent to argue against AI exceptionalism in audit design.
skeptic.summary: Endorses behavioral auditing as the empirically grounded, non-exceptional regulatory path.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Related to 'Aviation-to-AI Regulatory Transfer' and 'Component vs System Safety' but distinct: this node specifically frames the choice of output-behavior audit over input-scale gating as the affirmative regulatory model. Worth a dedicated node given all three converge on it for different reasons.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: Documented present-day harms (biased hiring screens, pretrial risk scores, tenant-screening models, low-paid content labeling) are not addressed by a compute gate and ride a separate instrument — uniform disclosure and incident-reporting standards.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns the institutional separation between compute-gating frontier regimes and the disclosure/incident-reporting instruments needed for existing documented harms. Encompasses: bias in deployed decision systems, labor harms in data labeling, the bifurcation of frontier-catastrophe vs present-harm tooling. Excludes: catastrophic capability concentration, audit-model selection, and licensing-power design.

accelerationist.belief: Today's documented harms come from deployed narrow systems and are unrelated to training-run scale.
accelerationist.desire: To keep frontier compute debates from absorbing or over-regulating ordinary deployed-system harms.
accelerationist.intention: Route present harms to lightweight disclosure rules, leaving frontier development unburdened.
accelerationist.summary: Separates present harms to prevent them from justifying heavy frontier compute controls.

safetyist.belief: Present-day and frontier risks are distinct failure classes requiring distinct instruments to address both adequately.
safetyist.desire: To ensure existing harms are remedied through disclosure and incident reporting without weakening frontier oversight.
safetyist.intention: Build a parallel disclosure-and-incident track so neither catastrophic nor present harms are neglected.
safetyist.summary: Supports a dedicated present-harm instrument as complementary to frontier safety controls.

skeptic.belief: The real, documented harms are present-day and structural, and compute gating distracts from addressing them.
skeptic.desire: To prioritize concrete remedies for demonstrated harms over speculative frontier regimes.
skeptic.intention: Push uniform disclosure and incident-reporting as the substantive, evidence-based intervention.
skeptic.summary: Treats present-harm disclosure as the priority instrument that compute gating wrongly displaces.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Related to 'Data-Driven Harms from AI Systems' and 'Aviation-Inspired AI Incident Reporting', but this agreement is specifically about the institutional bifurcation — that present harms ride a separate instrument from frontier compute gates. The split-instrument logic is novel.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: A licensing or halt authority is itself a concentration of power that can be captured, and any such regime must carry its own rollback — a fixed-clock statutory sunset and halt authority distributed across more than one body.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns guarding regulatory licensing/halt authority against capture through built-in rollback mechanisms — statutory sunsets and distributed authority across multiple bodies. Encompasses: regulator capture risk, sunset clauses, separation/distribution of halt power, institutional self-limitation. Excludes: the substance of what is being audited, fee structures, and present-harm instruments.

accelerationist.belief: A single licensing or halt body becomes a chokepoint that incumbents will capture to block competitors.
accelerationist.desire: To prevent any control regime from ossifying into a permanent innovation-suppressing gatekeeper.
accelerationist.intention: Insist on hard sunsets and split authority so any regime self-destructs absent renewal.
accelerationist.summary: Demands rollback design to stop licensing authority from entrenching as an anti-competitive chokepoint.

safetyist.belief: Even necessary safety authorities are vulnerable to capture, which erodes their protective function over time.
safetyist.desire: To make safety regimes durable and legitimate by insulating them from capture through distribution and review.
safetyist.intention: Distribute halt power and add sunset reviews so the regime remains trusted and renewable.
safetyist.summary: Accepts self-limitation to preserve the legitimacy and trustworthiness of safety authority.

skeptic.belief: Concentrated governance power is itself a major risk that tends to be captured and to outlive its justification.
skeptic.desire: To ensure no new authority can persist or expand without affirmative democratic re-authorization.
skeptic.intention: Hardwire fixed-clock sunsets and multi-body distribution to force periodic accountability.
skeptic.summary: Treats self-limiting rollback as essential because concentrated authority is inherently capture-prone.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Distinct from 'AI and Concentrated Power', 'The Power Mechanics Blind Spot', and 'Regulatory Lookback Mechanisms'. This node specifically addresses designing rollback (sunset + distributed halt) into the regulatory authority itself as a capture safeguard. The convergence on institutional self-limitation merits its own node.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: A safe harbor's evaluation requirement should include a statutory turnaround cap (ship-by-default if the body misses its window) and a fee scaled to developer capitalization and capability tier rather than a flat charge.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns procedural design of evaluation safe harbors — statutory turnaround caps with ship-by-default fallback and capitalization/capability-scaled fees rather than flat charges. Encompasses: regulator response-time limits, default-approval-on-delay rules, proportionate fee structures, small-developer burden mitigation. Excludes: which behaviors are evaluated, halt-authority rollback, and present-harm disclosure.

accelerationist.belief: Open-ended review windows and flat fees disproportionately strangle startups and open-source developers.
accelerationist.desire: To guarantee that regulatory delay never becomes a de facto ban and that small actors are not priced out.
accelerationist.intention: Lock in ship-by-default deadlines and capitalization-scaled fees to protect broad-based innovation.
accelerationist.summary: Backs ship-by-default and scaled fees to keep evaluation from becoming a barrier to entry.

safetyist.belief: A workable safe harbor needs reasonable timelines and funding to function without being gamed or starved.
safetyist.desire: To make evaluation administratively viable and adequately resourced while remaining proportionate.
safetyist.intention: Set turnaround caps and tier-scaled fees that sustain genuine review without inviting evasion.
safetyist.summary: Supports bounded timelines and scaled fees as the conditions for a functioning, resourced evaluation regime.

skeptic.belief: Without hard deadlines and proportionate fees, evaluation bodies drift into arbitrary, capturable bottlenecks.
skeptic.desire: To force accountability and fairness on the evaluating authority through enforceable procedural defaults.
skeptic.intention: Mandate statutory caps and capitalization-scaled fees to constrain bureaucratic discretion.
skeptic.summary: Endorses procedural defaults to keep evaluation bodies accountable and non-arbitrary.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Related to 'The Determination Time Gap', 'Regulatory Fragmentation and Cost Burden', and 'Authority-Bound Output Release' but distinct in its specific procedural prescription: ship-by-default turnaround caps plus capitalization-scaled fees. This concrete safe-harbor design proposal warrants a dedicated node.

accelerationist.recommendation: Consider adding more Desires nodes for the accelerationist perspective

safetyist.recommendation: Consider adding more Beliefs nodes for the safetyist perspective

skeptic.recommendation: Consider adding more Beliefs nodes for the skeptic perspective

summary.recommendation: Overall taxonomy coverage is 38% — many injected nodes go unused

config_summary.topic: Should frontier AI development be gated by compute-threshold licensing, and through what pathways would such a regime reshape the incentives of large labs, open-source developers, insurers, and national competitiveness — given the tension between preventing catastrophic capability concentration and chilling broad-based innovation?
